intro: To plan a multi-week unit with AI, start with what students must do by the last week. Then ask the AI tool for one week at a time, and check every draft against your standards before you keep it. This page covers the routine on a Mac, the time it really saves, the student data rules that apply, and where Lazur can explain, point, guide and draft with you.
tldr: Start with the end goal. Write what students must do by the last week, then work backward to week one.
Draft one week at a time with AI. Share only the student information your district allows for that tool.
Check each draft against your standards document, your pacing guide and your class before you keep it.
Save the finished unit as a Pages template so next year starts from structure, not a blank page.
Lazur explains what is on screen, points at menus, guides each click and drafts text. It does not click for you.

blocks.text: How to plan a multi-week unit with AI, step by step

Start before you open any AI tool. Open a blank Pages document and write one sentence for each thing students should be able to do when the unit ends. Those sentences are your targets. Every week in the plan has to lead to one of them.

items: Write the end goal. Keep the list short, and name what students will do, not what you will cover.
Decide the evidence. List the task, quiz or project that shows each goal.
Map the weeks. Put the goals in order and give each one a week. Leave room for review before the assessment.
Draft one week at a time. Give the AI tool the goal, the week topic and the evidence for that week only.
Check the draft. Compare it to your standards document, your pacing guide and your actual class.
Fold it into your template. Copy the structure into a saved Pages template and rewrite the wording in your own voice.
Revise after real lessons. Teach the first week, then fix the next week based on what your students showed you.

blocks.text: Ask for one week at a time. A whole unit in one prompt often comes back generic. Short requests give you specific lessons you can check line by line, which is the step most people skip.
A worked example: a unit on the water cycle

Say you teach a science unit on the water cycle. The end goal is that students can explain evaporation, condensation and precipitation with a labeled diagram of their own. The evidence is that diagram and a short written explanation at the end of the unit.

A good first prompt names the subject, the goal, the week and the materials you own. For example: draft the week on condensation for upper elementary science. Include a lesson focus, a hands-on activity and an exit question. Use only vocabulary from our current textbook chapter.

blocks.caption: The shape of one week in a unit plan, with the check you run before you keep it.

blocks.text: The table is a shape, not finished content. Fill each cell yourself, then ask the AI tool to tighten the wording. The shape keeps the draft from drifting into filler that sounds like a lesson but teaches nothing.
Stop the worked example at one week on purpose. Once the first week works, the rest of the unit usually follows the same shape. Check each new week before you draft the one after it.
What you can and cannot give an AI tool

Student data is the line most teachers worry about, and they should. Do not paste student names, IEP details, grades or health notes into an AI tool unless your district has approved that tool for that data. Follow your employer's rules on student records.

blocks.title: Student data first
blocks.text: Plan with topics, standards and general needs such as reading level or language support. Keep names, IEP details and grades out of the prompt unless your district approves the tool for that data.

Good inputs are the unit topic, the standard codes from a public standards document, the class periods you have, the materials you own, the reading level of your texts, and the assessments you already use. None of those identify a student.
Check the AI draft before it goes in your plan
An AI draft is a first pass. It can sound right and still fit your class badly. Read it as the teacher who will teach it on Monday, not as an editor checking grammar.

items: Check the standards. Open the official standards document and match each week to a real code.
Check the pacing. Ask whether the week fits your schedule, testing dates and school events.
Check the vocabulary. Compare every key term with the textbook or readings you already use.
Check the grading load. A project that needs long feedback for every student will not fit a normal week.
Check for students with support plans. Add general notes for them, without pasting their details into the tool.
Check every fact. Verify any date, name or statistic the draft gives you against a primary source.

blocks.text: If the draft names a standard or a fact, verify it against the official source. You can ask Lazur to research the public page and return a summary, then read the source yourself before you trust it.
Build a reusable unit template in Pages

Once the unit works, save its structure so next year starts from a template. In Pages, open the finished document and choose File > Save as Template. Then choose Add to Template Chooser to keep it in Pages, or Save to store it as a file.

items: Open the finished unit in Pages and clear the names, dates and any student details.
Keep the headings, the weekly table and the check boxes, because those carry the structure.
Choose File > Save as Template, then choose Add to Template Chooser or Save.
Next time, choose File > New and pick your template from My Templates, the last category in the template chooser.
To rename or delete it later, choose File > New, then Control-click the template name and pick Rename or Delete.

blocks.title: Pick a template on purpose
blocks.text: Hold Option while you choose File > New from the Template Chooser to pick a different template. To change the default for new documents, go to Pages > Settings > General, select Use template, and click Change Template.

Custom templates sync when iCloud Drive is on and you use the same Apple Account, but they do not sync to Pages for iCloud. Deleting a template removes it from all your devices when iCloud Drive is on. Built-in templates cannot be deleted.
Keep a small set of templates, one for each kind of unit you teach. A project unit and a skills unit need different tables. A few clear templates beat a folder full of near copies.
Pages or Google Docs for a unit plan

Use Pages if you work on a Mac and want the template to live on your machine. Use Google Docs if your team edits together in a browser. The routine above works in either app. Read more in [Pages for teachers](/for/teachers/pages) and [Google Docs for teachers](/for/teachers/google-docs).
How much time AI really saves on unit plans

Teachers say they lack planning time, and the numbers back that up. A national survey reported by NCTQ found 84% of teachers do not believe they have enough time during regular work hours for tasks like grading and lesson planning.

Districts give 40 to 480 minutes of planning time a week, depending on district and grade level. The most common allotment is 3.5 to 4 hours. Across a common set of districts, that figure has been essentially flat over the last decade.

The Gallup and Walton Family Foundation survey from 2025 found that teachers who use AI at least weekly report saving 5.9 hours a week. Monthly users report 2.9 hours. Those figures are self-reported, and teachers may not count the time they spend checking AI output.
If a tool saves you a long drafting session but adds a long checking session, the net gain is small. Time your own first unit with and without AI before you decide.
Where the time goes in a normal teacher week

The EdWeek Research Center survey from 2022 found the median teacher works 54 hours a week in total. That teacher spends 5 hours planning or preparing and 2 hours collaborating with colleagues on planning. The survey's sample size is not stated on the page.

OECD data, as NCTQ reports it, puts U.S. teachers at 5.1 hours a week on lesson planning and preparation, against 5.4 hours across OECD countries. NCTQ suggests U.S. teachers may make up limited planning time with hours outside the workday.
Those evening and weekend hours are a cost you pay at home. Plan the unit in the time you have, and be honest about what the rest of the week can absorb.
Share a unit plan with your team

Collaborative planning gets attention for a reason. NCTQ reports that 55% of 2025 Pathfinder districts require or permit it across all grade levels. Another 13% specify it for some levels, most often elementary.

NCTQ also cites earlier studies that link frequent instructional collaboration to higher reading and math gains. It cites Farbman (2015) as suggesting even one hour of collaborative planning a week can support positive outcomes. Those are secondhand summaries, so read the originals before you quote them.

Send the draft to one colleague by [Gmail](/for/teachers/gmail) before your planning meeting. Name the unit and the week in the subject line. Ask for marks on the weeks that do not fit the pacing guide.

For line-level feedback, use comments inside the document. In Google Docs, follow [how to add a comment](/how-to/add-a-comment-in-google-docs). In Pages, follow [how to add a comment](/how-to/add-a-comment-in-pages).
Mistakes teachers make with AI unit plans

items: Asking for the whole unit in one prompt, then accepting the first draft.
Pasting student names or IEP details into a tool your district has not approved.
Skipping the standards check because the draft sounds official.
Planning every lesson in detail, then running out of time to teach the plan.
Saving the finished plan as a file with no template, so next year starts from zero.
Squeezing the review and assessment weeks into the last few days.
Letting the AI choose vocabulary without comparing it to your textbook.

blocks.text: Edge cases: when to plan the unit yourself
Some parts of a unit should come from you. Assessments that count toward a grade need your judgment and your school's rules. So do the accommodations for students who have support plans.

Use AI for the skeleton, not the core. Write the key questions, the success criteria and the final assessment yourself. A unit built around a weak assessment stays weak, however neat the weekly table looks.
Watch for units that cross subjects or grade bands. A draft may miss the reading level your students use in a second subject. Check each text against what your students can read on their own.
If your district supplies a required curriculum, the draft has to fit it. Paste in only the materials you are allowed to share, and expect to rewrite the parts that clash with the required sequence.
Start this routine this week
Pick one unit you teach in the next few weeks. Write its end goal in a Pages document, then draft only the first week with AI. Check that week against your standards before the day you teach it.
Save the structure as a template before the week ends. Then draft the next week from the template, not from memory. The second draft usually goes faster than the first.

If you want help while you work, hold ⌥⌘ and ask about anything on screen. Hold fn to dictate your own notes at the cursor in any app. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel. Windows is planned, not available. See [pricing](/pricing) for plans, or [download Lazur](/download).

faq.question: Can AI plan a whole multi-week unit for me?
faq.answer: It can draft one. Treat the result as a first pass. You still decide the end goal, the final assessment and what fits your class. Draft one week at a time, and check each week against your standards document before you use it.

faq.question: Is it safe to paste student information into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Not unless your district allows that tool for that kind of data. Follow your employer's rules on student records. Describe needs in general terms, such as reading level, and keep names, IEP details and grades out of the prompt.

faq.question: How much time does AI save on unit planning?
faq.answer: The best figure is self-reported. Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation found that teachers who use AI at least weekly report saving 5.9 hours a week. Teachers may not count the time they spend checking AI output, so the figure may overstate savings.

faq.question: How do I save a unit plan as a template in Pages on Mac?
faq.answer: Open the finished document and choose File > Save as Template. Choose Add to Template Chooser to keep it in Pages, or Save to store it as a file. Next time, choose File > New and pick it from My Templates.

faq.question: How do I change the template Pages uses for new documents?
faq.answer: Go to Pages > Settings > General, select Use template, and click Change Template. To pick a different template for one document, hold Option while you choose File > New from the Template Chooser.

faq.question: Does Lazur write my unit plan in Pages?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts text, explains what is on screen, points at menu items and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons or operate Pages for you. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about your screen.

faq.question: Can Lazur check my unit against my state standards?
faq.answer: Lazur can research public pages in its own Chrome tabs and return a summary and a report. You still read the official standards document yourself and decide what matches your plan.

costs.title: Your evenings and weekends
costs.text: Planning a unit from a blank page takes time you may not have in the school day. The 2022 EdWeek survey puts the median teacher at 54 hours a week in total, with 5 hours on planning or preparing. The rest goes to teaching, grading and everything else.

costs.title: Planning that spills past work hours
costs.text: A national survey reported by NCTQ found 84% of teachers do not believe they have enough time during regular work hours for tasks like grading and lesson planning. Planning often spills into evenings and weekends, where it competes with rest.

costs.title: A gap that shows up in class
costs.text: A rushed plan has holes. Week three may repeat week two, or the final assessment may test something you never taught. You find those gaps in front of students, when you cannot fix them on a Sunday night.

costs.title: Student data exposure
costs.text: Pasting student details into an AI tool your district has not approved can break rules on student records. The cost can be a difficult conversation with an administrator, and a policy problem for your whole school.

costs.title: Duplicated work across the team
costs.text: When each teacher builds a unit alone, the team repeats the same planning. Many districts require or permit collaborative planning, according to NCTQ. One shared draft often gives the whole team a place to start.

causes.title: Planning time is short and flat
causes.text: Districts give 40 to 480 minutes of planning time a week, depending on district and grade level. The most common allotment is 3.5 to 4 hours. NCTQ reports that this figure has been essentially flat over the last decade, so the time does not grow with the job.

causes.title: The school day interrupts planning
causes.text: Teachers often report being pulled away from planning time for duties such as lunch monitoring or covering absent colleagues. A unit plan needs long stretches of uninterrupted thinking, and the school day rarely gives them to you.

causes.title: A blank page costs decisions
causes.text: The first version of any unit starts from a blank page. You decide the goal, the sequence, the evidence and the pacing at the same time. That load of decisions is why many units stall before the first lesson.

causes.title: Standards documents are dense
causes.text: Standards documents list many codes, and the wording often overlaps. Matching each week to the right codes takes careful reading. That step is easy to skip when time is short, and skipping it is how gaps appear.

causes.title: Good structures stay in one file
causes.text: Many teachers rebuild their structure each year because the finished plan lives in a file no one can find. Without a reusable template, last year's work does not carry over to the next unit or the next year.

causes.title: Generic AI drafts lack your context
causes.text: A general AI tool does not know your class, your pacing guide or your students unless you tell it. The result can read well and still fit poorly. The gap is context, not writing quality, so the fix is more context.

causes.title: Checking AI output is easy to forget
causes.text: Self-reported savings from AI may overstate the gain, since teachers may not count the time they spend checking output. Checking is real work. It belongs in your estimate of what a tool saves you.

fixes.title: Write the end goal before anything else
fixes.text: Write one sentence per outcome in a blank Pages document. Name what students will do, not what you will cover. Every week must lead to one of those sentences. If a lesson does not, cut it or move it to a later week.

fixes.title: Draft one week at a time
fixes.text: Give the AI tool the end goal, the topic of one week and the evidence for that week. Ask for a short outline with a lesson focus, a hands-on activity and an exit question. Repeat for each week. Short requests produce drafts you can check.

fixes.title: Check against the official standards document
fixes.text: Open the standards document your state or district publishes. Match each week to a real standard code. Delete any code that does not appear in the document. The check takes minutes, and it catches errors that a fluent draft hides.

fixes.title: Keep student details out of the prompt
fixes.text: Describe needs in general terms, such as reading level, language support or pace. Keep names, IEP details, grades and health notes out of the tool. If you need a tailored version, do that work in a system your district has approved for student data, if one exists.

fixes.title: Build the template once, then reuse it
fixes.text: Save the finished structure with File > Save as Template in Pages. Clear the names and dates first. For the next unit, choose File > New and pick your template from My Templates. You start with the table, not a blank page.

fixes.title: Plan the assessment and review weeks first
fixes.text: Put the final assessment on the calendar before you write the lessons. Then work backward from it. Reserve a review week before the test, so the plan does not end in a rush and the review does not get cut.

fixes.title: Use a colleague as the second check
fixes.text: Send the draft to one colleague before your planning meeting. Ask them to mark any week that does not fit the pacing guide. Specific marks are faster to act on than a long meeting, and they catch what you stopped seeing.

fixes.title: Time the routine and keep your own numbers
fixes.text: Track how long your first AI-assisted unit takes, and how long a unit without AI takes. Write the minutes in a note inside the template. Your own numbers tell you more than a survey average, because they include your checking time.

plan.label: Sunday
plan.title: Write the goal and the assessment
plan.text: Open a blank Pages document. Write the unit end goal and the final assessment in your own words. Draft nothing else until those two lines are clear.

plan.label: Monday
plan.title: Draft and check the first week
plan.text: Give the AI tool the goal and the evidence for the first week only. Compare the draft to your standards document and pacing guide, then mark what needs a real change.

plan.label: Tuesday
plan.title: Rewrite in your own voice
plan.text: Make the changes yourself. Hold fn to dictate notes at the cursor if talking is faster than typing. Keep the week as a section you can copy into the next unit later.

plan.label: Thursday
plan.title: Get one colleague to check it
plan.text: Email the draft to one colleague with the unit and week in the subject line. Ask for marks on any week that does not fit. Set an Apple Reminders item for the planning meeting.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Save the structure and log the time
plan.text: Save the structure as a Pages template with File > Save as Template. Write down how long the week took. Choose the next week to draft on Monday, and start from the template.
